points_of_disagreement: Whether Iran's refusal is primarily a rational deterrence strategy (Sovereignty framing) or a tactical negotiating position (Leverage framing) or an ideological commitment (Nuclear Security framing).
Whether the 2018 JCPOA withdrawal was the proximate cause of HEU buildup (Failed Diplomacy framing) or whether Iran's enrichment was inevitable regardless (Nuclear Security framing).
Whether military force is a viable option (Nuclear Security framing) or operationally fraught and counterproductive (Military Seizure Viability framing).
Whether the impasse reflects Iran's untrustworthiness (Nuclear Security framing) or US policy failure (Failed Diplomacy framing).
Whether the HEU stockpile is primarily a proliferation threat (Nuclear Security framing) or a legitimate deterrent against regime change (Sovereignty framing).
Whether the standoff is accelerating NPT collapse (Non-Proliferation Regime Collapse framing) or is a contained bilateral dispute (other framings).
Whether verification of any transfer agreement is possible given IAEA access loss (Verification Breakdown framing) or whether alternative verification methods exist (implied in Leverage framing).
Whether domestic US politics is distorting the response (Political Fallout framing) or whether substantive nuclear security concerns are primary (Nuclear Security framing).
shared_foundation.summary: All framings accept that Iran has refused to transfer HEU to the US, that Iran possesses highly enriched uranium at ~60% purity, that the JCPOA was abandoned in 2018, that military strikes occurred in June 2025, and that IAEA verification access has been lost. The disagreements are entirely about causation (what led to this impasse), interpretation (what Iran's refusal means strategically and morally), and remedy (whether diplomacy, military action, or structural reform is appropriate).

framings.name: Nuclear Security Threat
framings.question: Does Iran's refusal to transfer its HEU constitute an ongoing and unacceptable threat to global and regional security?
framings.key_claim: Iran's refusal to surrender its HEU stockpile—enough for over ten nuclear warheads—leaves the world at imminent proliferation risk and validates the use of maximum pressure, including military force.
framings.description: This framing treats Iran's HEU stockpile as the central security danger of the era. It foregrounds the quantitative bomb-making potential of the stockpile and frames Iran's refusal as proof of malign intent, justifying escalatory US-Israeli responses.
framings.emphasizes: The near-weapons-grade level of enrichment (60%), the theoretical bomb-making capacity of 440+ kg, Iran's breakout timeline, Khamenei's directive against transfer, and the inadequacy of diplomacy.
framings.downplays: Iran's stated civilian justifications, IAEA assessments that Iran had not reauthorized a weapons program, the role of US JCPOA withdrawal in producing the stockpile, and the risks of military escalation.
sample_headlines: Trump says US will not allow Iran to reach enriched uranium
Iran's HEU stockpile: Enough for 10+ nuclear warheads

carriers.name: Donald Trump / White House
carriers.excerpt: "We will get it. We don't need it. We don't want it. We'll probably destroy it after we get it, but we're not going to let them have it."
carriers.role_evidence: Trump personally articulated this framing in repeated White House statements and on social media, anchoring the entire US policy posture around the HEU threat.

carriers.name: Times of Israel
carriers.excerpt: Khamenei said to refuse to give up stockpile of near-weapons grade nuclear material, which US and Israel have demanded be confiscated before war can end.
carriers.role_evidence: Prominently amplified the security-threat framing by foregrounding Israeli officials' insistence that HEU removal is a non-negotiable war-ending condition.

carriers.name: Benjamin Netanyahu / Israeli Government
carriers.excerpt: Netanyahu has said he will not consider the war over until enriched uranium is removed from Iran.
carriers.role_evidence: Israeli government formally adopted the HEU transfer as a hard precondition to any ceasefire, institutionalizing this framing at the highest level.

carriers.name: Steve Witkoff / US Special Envoy
carriers.excerpt: Witkoff stated that Iran's uranium enrichment facilities must be dismantled for Washington to believe its claim of not seeking nuclear weapons.
carriers.role_evidence: As chief US negotiator, Witkoff repeatedly amplified this framing in public statements, driving mainstream US media coverage.

carriers.name: Pete Hegseth / US Secretary of Defense
carriers.excerpt: Hegseth said that Iran would be capable of nuclear blackmail with their ballistic missiles if the US did not attack it.
carriers.role_evidence: Used the nuclear threat framing to publicly justify launching the 2026 military campaign.

framings.name: Iranian Sovereignty and Deterrence Logic
framings.question: Is Iran's refusal to transfer HEU a rational act of national self-defense by a country that has been repeatedly attacked?
framings.key_claim: Iran's refusal to surrender its HEU is a predictable and strategically rational assertion of sovereignty, particularly given that relinquishing the stockpile would remove its primary deterrent against further US-Israeli military aggression.
framings.description: This framing treats the HEU stockpile as Iran's strategic leverage, not evidence of weapons intent. It contextualizes the refusal within a pattern of US and Israeli attacks, treaty violations, and a history of targeted killings, arguing that any state would make the same calculation.
framings.emphasizes: Iran's vulnerability to repeated attack, Khamenei's logic that transferring HEU = invitation for further strikes, Iran's NPT membership and stated civilian nuclear rights, and the deterrence value of the stockpile.
framings.downplays: The genuine proliferation dangers of 60%-enriched uranium stockpiles, Iran's history of concealed nuclear activities, and IAEA findings of undeclared nuclear work.
sample_headlines: "Enriched uranium is as sacred to us as Iranian soil and will not be transferred anywhere under any circumstances"
Trump wonders why Iran won't 'capitulate' on its nuclear program. Here's why.

carriers.name: Esmaeil Baghaei / Iran Foreign Ministry
carriers.excerpt: "Enriched uranium is as sacred to us as Iranian soil and will not be transferred anywhere under any circumstances."
carriers.role_evidence: The Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson coined the most quotable statement of this framing, circulated globally.

carriers.name: CNN
carriers.excerpt: For Tehran, the nuclear program is about its identity as a modern nation.
carriers.role_evidence: Ran a widely-read analytical explainer foregrounding the deterrence and sovereignty logic behind Iran's nuclear posture.

carriers.name: Al Jazeera
carriers.excerpt: Iranian officials have stated they are open to discussing reducing the level of enrichment... but have refused to dismantle Iran's nuclear programme entirely, a matter of national sovereignty, they say.
carriers.role_evidence: Consistently foregrounded Iran's own framing of sovereignty and deterrence, including expert voices supporting the strategic logic.

carriers.name: Jeffrey Lewis / Middlebury Institute
carriers.excerpt: Lewis said Iran was "likely to reach the same conclusion that North Korea reached, that it's a dangerous world out there with the United States, and it's better to go nuclear."
carriers.role_evidence: Academic expert articulating the deterrence logic that undergirds this framing, cited widely.

carriers.name: Times of Israel (Iranian sources)
carriers.excerpt: Iran's top officials believe that sending the material abroad would leave the country more vulnerable to future attacks.
carriers.role_evidence: Relayed the Iranian establishment's internal deterrence rationale, even while editorially aligned with the threat framing.

framings.name: Non-Proliferation Regime Collapse
framings.question: Does Iran's HEU impasse—combined with US-Israeli military strikes—signal the irreversible breakdown of the global nuclear non-proliferation architecture?
framings.key_claim: The standoff over Iran's HEU, caused as much by the US withdrawal from the JCPOA and subsequent military strikes as by Iran's refusal, is accelerating the collapse of the NPT framework and incentivizing other states to pursue nuclear weapons.
framings.description: This framing, most prominent among arms control experts and academic institutions, focuses on systemic damage. It argues Iran's refusal is a downstream consequence of a broken diplomatic chain, and that the entire episode undermines the logic of non-proliferation bargains worldwide.
framings.emphasizes: The JCPOA's demolition by the 2018 US withdrawal, the precedent-setting nature of attacking a non-nuclear-armed NPT signatory, Iran's potential NPT exit, and global proliferation cascades.
framings.downplays: Iran's own sustained breach of JCPOA limits after 2019 and IAEA findings of undeclared nuclear activities.
sample_headlines: How the Iran War undermines the nuclear nonproliferation regime
The US-Israeli War on Iran Is Incentivizing Nuclear Proliferation

carriers.name: Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists
carriers.excerpt: The war raises doubts that the Non-Proliferation Treaty can hold as a central pillar of international security.
carriers.role_evidence: Published multiple expert analyses originating and sustaining this framing, including moving the Doomsday Clock to 85 seconds to midnight.

carriers.name: Stimson Center
carriers.excerpt: Iran reportedly mulls withdrawing altogether from the Treaty on the Nonproliferation of Nuclear Weapons, raising questions about global nonproliferation architecture.
carriers.role_evidence: Curated and amplified expert analysis on NPT fragmentation as a direct result of the Iran conflict and HEU standoff.

carriers.name: Arms Control Association / Kelsey Davenport
carriers.excerpt: Kelsey Davenport, Director for Nonproliferation Policy at the Arms Control Association, analyzed US-Israeli attacks against Iran and concerns around Iran's nuclear program.
carriers.role_evidence: Leading expert voice amplifying the NPT-collapse framing in public panels and publications.

carriers.name: IISS (International Institute for Strategic Studies)
carriers.excerpt: History shows a range of risks in kinetic approaches and suggests that the Iranian nuclear question will likely remain unresolved in the longer term.
carriers.role_evidence: Published authoritative analysis arguing military counter-proliferation undermines rather than resolves the NPT framework.

carriers.name: Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation
carriers.excerpt: Iran's HEU stockpile is now over 400 kg enriched to 60% — a nearly 50% increase since February, raising concerns that a future agreement would face serious verification challenges.
carriers.role_evidence: Maintained running factsheets used by journalists and policymakers, grounding this framing in documented evidence.

framings.name: Failed US Diplomacy / Own Goal
framings.question: Did US policy choices—especially the 2018 JCPOA withdrawal and the decision to strike Iran during active talks—directly produce the HEU impasse Iran now refuses to resolve?
framings.key_claim: The US manufactured the very crisis it is now trying to solve: the 2018 JCPOA withdrawal caused Iran to build its HEU stockpile, and launching military strikes during negotiations destroyed the diplomatic trust needed to transfer it.
framings.description: This framing, common in liberal and arms-control circles and among Democratic lawmakers, argues that Iran's refusal is largely a consequence of US credibility destruction. Iran cannot trust US deal-keeping after the JCPOA experience, making transfer demands unrealistic without ironclad guarantees.
framings.emphasizes: Trump's 2018 withdrawal as the proximate cause of HEU buildup, US strikes launched while negotiations were active, Iran's reasonable demand for guarantees against future US withdrawal, and Democratic congressional criticism.
framings.downplays: Iran's own deliberate escalation of enrichment beyond JCPOA limits, IAEA findings of undeclared activities, and Iran's strategic use of the stockpile as leverage.
sample_headlines: Iran's HEU stockpile is the consequence of Trump's decision in 2018 to withdraw from a multilateral nuclear deal
Sen. Booker: 'Donald Trump is being played as a fool that he is for getting us into this in the first place'

carriers.name: Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ)
carriers.excerpt: "What I'm seeing that has me so outraged right now is the president said he went into this to deal with their nuclear program. This does not deal with that."
carriers.role_evidence: High-profile Democratic lawmaker used national TV to advance this framing, criticizing Trump for failing the very goals he claimed to enter the war to achieve.

carriers.name: Wikipedia / Rationale for the 2026 Iran War (citing multiple analysts)
carriers.excerpt: Iran's development of HEU stockpile itself is the consequence of Trump's decision in 2018 to withdraw from a multilateral nuclear deal.
carriers.role_evidence: Aggregates and reflects the 'own goal' framing as a prominent analytical lens in the mainstream record.

carriers.name: CNN Politics
carriers.excerpt: Both conservative hawks and Democrats seem to believe he's on the cusp of caving to a bad deal.
carriers.role_evidence: Ran analytical framing that foregrounded the bipartisan view that US policy created the current impasse.

carriers.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD)
carriers.excerpt: Van Hollen warned the proposed agreement would "take us back to the prewar status quo" or worse.
carriers.role_evidence: Used congressional platform to argue US diplomatic failures were central to the HEU impasse.

carriers.name: Obama White House Archives
carriers.excerpt: Under the JCPOA, Iran must reduce its stockpile of uranium by 98% and will keep its level of uranium enrichment at 3.67%.
carriers.role_evidence: JCPOA documentation serves as the evidentiary foundation against which the 'own goal' framing measures US policy failure.

framings.name: Negotiating Leverage / Transactional Impasse
framings.question: Is Iran's HEU refusal primarily a bargaining chip to extract maximum concessions—sanctions relief, security guarantees, and economic benefits—rather than a principled red line?
framings.key_claim: Iran is using its HEU stockpile as strategic leverage in a high-stakes transaction; the refusal to transfer is not ideological but tactical, designed to extract binding security guarantees and economic compensation before surrendering its most valuable negotiating asset.
framings.description: This framing, common in diplomatic and foreign policy analysis, treats Iran's refusal as rational bargaining behavior. It focuses on the sequencing of concessions, the gap between US and Iranian timelines, and Iran's demand for ironclad guarantees before any transfer.
framings.emphasizes: Iran's offer to dilute rather than transfer, its demand for exit-clause protections, the 60-day negotiating window, Pakistan/Saudi/Egypt as facilitators, and the economic dimension (sanctions relief, oil exports).
framings.downplays: Genuine ideological dimensions of the refusal (sovereignty, identity, regime survival) and the military escalation risks of prolonged transactionalism.
sample_headlines: Iran ready to dilute enriched uranium, rejects transfer abroad
Scoop: U.S. nuclear deal offer allows Iran to enrich uranium
Details emerge about potential Iran deal as Trump says not to rush

carriers.name: Reuters (citing unnamed Iranian/Israeli sources)
carriers.excerpt: The supreme leader's directive and the consensus within the establishment are that the stockpile of enriched uranium should not leave the country.
carriers.role_evidence: Reuters was first to report the internal Iranian logic framing HEU retention as a negotiating and security calculus, not a flat refusal.

carriers.name: Axios
carriers.excerpt: Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said the U.S. side had so far not provided sufficient assurances in terms of when and how sanctions would be lifted.
carriers.role_evidence: Broke scoops on the gap between US offers and Iranian demands, framing the HEU issue as a transactional impasse.

carriers.name: Iran International
carriers.excerpt: Iran is prepared to downblend its highly enriched uranium stockpile to 3.7% and 20% levels but has refused to transfer the material outside the country.
carriers.role_evidence: Reported the compromise offer—dilution vs. transfer—highlighting Iran's willingness to negotiate terms, framing refusal as strategic rather than absolute.

carriers.name: CNBC
carriers.excerpt: Tehran proposed separate negotiations and offered to dilute some of its highly enriched uranium and transfer the rest to a third country, with a provision that it be returned if Washington exits any eventual deal.
carriers.role_evidence: Major financial/business outlet framed Iran's HEU position as a complex transactional negotiation with exit-clause protection demands.

carriers.name: Chatham House / Sanam Vakil
carriers.excerpt: "Tehran sees zero enrichment as a strategic red line and is betting that Washington will ultimately accept limits as it has in the past rather than risk escalation."
carriers.role_evidence: Chatham House expert framed Iran's position as a calculated strategic bet on US risk aversion, consistent with the transactional lens.

framings.name: Military Seizure Viability
framings.question: Can the United States realistically seize or destroy Iran's HEU stockpile by force, and what are the physical, radiological, and strategic risks of trying?
framings.key_claim: Forcibly removing Iran's HEU stockpile—whether by commando raid, further airstrikes, or excavation—is technically and operationally fraught, and military attempts may scatter, obscure, or never fully account for the material.
framings.description: This framing is primarily driven by security analysts, nuclear scientists, and defense journalists. It interrogates the feasibility of the US military option as an alternative to negotiated transfer, concluding that force is an unreliable solution to the HEU problem.
framings.emphasizes: The toxicity and dispersal risks of uranium hexafluoride gas, the underground location of the stockpile, IAEA access loss since June 2025, the precedent of failed historical counter-proliferation raids, and IRGC protection of the material.
framings.downplays: The diplomatic pathways and their potential efficacy; the political dimension of why military seizure is being seriously contemplated.
sample_headlines: Can the US seize Iran's enriched uranium – and what are the risks?
Iran's enriched uranium stockpile: Can it be safely transferred?

carriers.name: Al Jazeera
carriers.excerpt: Placing boots on the ground to seize or neutralise the HEU, in hostile territory with unclear intelligence, is fraught with risk.
carriers.role_evidence: Published one of the first and most comprehensive analyses of military seizure risks, drawing on nuclear scientists and former US officials.

carriers.name: Al Jazeera (safety transfer explainer)
carriers.excerpt: Uranium hexafluoride gas is extremely dangerous. If released, it can form highly toxic and corrosive fluoride compounds.
carriers.role_evidence: Ran detailed explainer on physical and logistical risks of HEU transfer, widely shared globally.

carriers.name: CBS News / 60 Minutes
carriers.excerpt: "I don't think that there is a lasting, durable solution to Iran's nuclear program through military means."
carriers.role_evidence: 60 Minutes prime-time episode brought the viability framing to a mass American audience, featuring former NNSA and national lab experts.

carriers.name: IISS
carriers.excerpt: On a strategic level, the use of force to counter nuclear programmes can incentivise states to continue to pursue nuclear weapons.
carriers.role_evidence: Provided authoritative strategic-level analysis of kinetic counter-proliferation risks, shaping elite policy debate.

carriers.name: Stimson Center / Joseph Rodgers
carriers.excerpt: The operation to seize Iran's stockpile of near-weapons-grade enriched uranium would require a significant ground presence.
carriers.role_evidence: Stimson Center expert directly challenged the viability of the military seizure option.

framings.name: Political Fallout and Domestic Politicization
framings.question: How is Iran's HEU refusal being exploited domestically—by Trump, Democrats, hawks, and doves—to advance competing political agendas regardless of the underlying nuclear facts?
framings.key_claim: Iran's HEU impasse has become a Rorschach test in US domestic politics: hawks say it proves Iran can never be trusted; Trump critics say it proves the war was a blunder; Trump allies say any deal will be a 'win'; all sides are performing for domestic audiences more than solving the nuclear problem.
framings.description: This meta-framing, most visible in political media and analysis, focuses on how the event is weaponized domestically. It notes the irony that conservative hawks AND Democratic critics both simultaneously accuse Trump of 'caving' to a bad deal, revealing that each side's nuclear concerns are partly pretextual.
framings.emphasizes: Congressional reactions, midterm politics, Trump's contradictory statements ('I don't care' vs. 'We will get it'), bipartisan accusations of deal weakness, and the Strait of Hormuz economic angle.
framings.downplays: The substantive technical and strategic merits of the underlying nuclear dispute.
sample_headlines: Analysis: Why a possible Iran deal may be almost as divisive as Trump's decision to wage war
The Iran war is hostage to bitter politics, entrenched ideologies

carriers.name: CNN Politics
carriers.excerpt: The Iran war, like everything else in Washington, is hostage to bitter politics, entrenched ideologies and politicians seeking to boost their own profiles.
carriers.role_evidence: Published a prominent analytical piece explicitly mapping the domestic political exploitation of the Iran HEU standoff across the political spectrum.

carriers.name: Wikipedia / Rationale for the 2026 Iran War (critics section)
carriers.excerpt: Some critics have described the United States intervention against Iran as a diversionary war, noting mounting domestic pressures including intense public scrutiny.
carriers.role_evidence: Aggregates the 'diversionary war' hypothesis, connecting the HEU issue to Trump's domestic political calculations.

carriers.name: Kevin Hassett / Trump National Economic Council
carriers.excerpt: Hassett told Fox News that a deal would unleash a "gusher" of oil through the strait.
carriers.role_evidence: Trump economic aide reframed the HEU/nuclear issue as an economic 'win' narrative for the domestic audience, illustrating the political exploitation dynamic.

carriers.name: Marco Rubio / US Secretary of State
carriers.excerpt: "The idea that somehow this president is going to agree to a deal that ultimately winds up putting Iran in a stronger position when it comes to nuclear ambitions is absurd."
carriers.role_evidence: Rubio's rebuttal of deal critics on a foreign trip was clearly calibrated for domestic political audiences.

framings.name: Verification and Transparency Breakdown
framings.question: With IAEA inspectors expelled since June 2025, does anyone actually know where Iran's HEU is, how much survives, and whether any transfer or dilution could be verified?
framings.key_claim: The entire HEU transfer debate is occluded by a fundamental epistemic problem: IAEA access has been blocked since the June 2025 strikes, meaning the international community cannot verify Iran's stockpile locations, quantities, or condition—making any deal's nuclear provisions essentially unverifiable.
framings.description: This framing, emphasized by technical arms-control experts and the IAEA itself, argues that the core precondition for any HEU deal—reliable knowledge of what exists and where—has been destroyed by the military escalation. It challenges both hawkish seizure plans and diplomatic transfer proposals on factual grounds.
framings.emphasizes: The IAEA inspection blackout since June 2025, uncertainty over what survived strikes, satellite imagery limitations, Iran's possible concealment, and the IAEA's acknowledgment of 'inaccessible' sites.
framings.downplays: The political will dimensions of the impasse; assumes facts could be ascertained if politics allowed.
sample_headlines: What Do We Actually Know About Iran's Nuclear Program? Not Much.
IAEA: Iran's stockpile remains 'mainly' stored in tunnel complex in Isfahan

carriers.name: Stimson Center / Samuel Hickey
carriers.excerpt: The loss of IAEA access since mid-2025 means the international community lacks verifiable knowledge about uranium locations and centrifuge capacity.
carriers.role_evidence: Directly originated the verification blackout framing as a core obstacle to resolving the HEU dispute.

carriers.name: IAEA / Rafael Grossi
carriers.excerpt: IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said the stockpile was 'mainly' stored in a tunnel complex in its Isfahan nuclear facility, and that his agency believed slightly more than 200 kg of it was there.
carriers.role_evidence: IAEA's own qualified, hedged language ('mainly,' 'believed') institutionally confirmed the verification gap.

carriers.name: CBS News / 60 Minutes
carriers.excerpt: International inspectors have not been allowed to verify Iran's stockpile since last June, when the U.S. and Israel struck three nuclear sites.
carriers.role_evidence: Brought the verification-blackout framing to a mass prime-time American audience.

carriers.name: Congressional Research Service (Paul K. Kerr)
carriers.excerpt: The IAEA withdrew inspectors from Iran in June 2025, and agency inspectors have not been able to inspect the attacked Iranian nuclear facilities.
carriers.role_evidence: CRS nonpartisan briefing for Congress formally documented the inspection blackout, giving the verification framing legislative authority.

carriers.name: Arms Control Association / Kelsey Davenport
carriers.excerpt: Although strikes can set back Iran's nuclear infrastructure, military force cannot eliminate Tehran's long-term proliferation risk because the country retains nuclear expertise and likely the key materials.
carriers.role_evidence: ACA's expert analysis consistently emphasized that without verified accounting of remaining HEU, military or diplomatic solutions are operating in the dark.

gap_analysis: Missing: the technical/scientific framing examining whether transfer is even operationally feasible or what the actual proliferation risk timeline is (vs. rhetorical urgency). Missing: Gulf state and Israeli security perspectives on Iran's uranium stockpile as a direct threat to their interests. Missing: the economic/sanctions angle—how uranium transfer relates to sanctions relief negotiations or JCPOA restoration economics. Missing: the domestic Iranian political economy view—why Iran's nuclear program has become non-negotiable domestically regardless of external pressure, and what constituencies depend on it.
